lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Choose one narrow learning theme for the week, define one visible result for Friday, and complete at least one small practice rep on each day you work on it.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Did I complete one practice rep? What was the main friction, and what should I change for the next rep?

faq.question: How narrow should the weekly theme be?
faq.answer: Narrow enough that you can name one visible result for Friday and one small practice rep for today. If either is vague, shrink the theme.

faq.question: What if I miss a planned practice day?
faq.answer: Resume with the next small rep. Do not compensate by making the next session larger; keep the weekly result reachable.

faq.question: When should I change the theme?
faq.answer: Review it at the end of the week. Keep it if the next step is still useful, narrow it if the scope is too broad, or replace it if the theme no longer matters.

intro.html: A weekly theme is a simple constraint for learning: choose one narrow skill, define one result you can inspect at the end of the week, and spend the week making small attempts around it. The point is not to finish a subject. The point is to create enough focused practice to learn what the next step should be.

sections.title: 1. Set the week
sections.html:
Name a theme that describes a small skill rather than a broad subject. Then define one Friday artifact: a short recording, a solved example, a small script, a sketch, a conversation practice, or another result you can inspect.

  • Theme: one narrow skill.
  • Friday result: one visible artifact or demonstration.
  • Inputs: start with up to three useful resources instead of collecting an unlimited reading list.

sections.title: 2. Use a small daily practice loop
sections.html:
When you work on the theme, begin with a small attempt. After the attempt, note the main friction. Use that friction to decide what to read, watch, ask, or practice next.

  1. Attempt a small rep.
  2. Write one sentence about what was difficult or unclear.
  3. Use one relevant input if it helps with that specific friction.
  4. Try again when useful.

The rep can be short. The useful unit is an attempt you can learn from, not a heroic session that makes tomorrow harder to start.

sections.title: 3. Adjust the scope, not the promise
sections.html: If the week becomes crowded, reduce the Friday result rather than widening the theme or abandoning it. A smaller finished artifact gives you something concrete to review. If you cannot name the next rep, the theme is probably still too broad.

sections.title: 4. Review on Friday
sections.html:
Close the week with a short review:

  • What can I do now that was harder at the start of the week?
  • What friction kept appearing?
  • Should I continue this theme, narrow it, or choose a different one?

The review is the finish line. The goal is not a streak; it is a clearer next decision.

sections.title: 5. Use Brali as the record
sections.html: Keep the theme as a short note or goal, put practice reps into your tasks or Focus sessions, and use a check-in or journal note to capture the main friction. At the end of the week, review that record before deciding what to do next.

lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Pick one concrete outcome, work on it for one 25-minute focus block, take a short break, and then decide whether another block is useful. Treat 25 minutes as a starting setting, not a scientifically optimal duration.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Did I work on the intended outcome? What interrupted me, and should the next focus block be shorter, the same, or longer?

faq.question: Why start with 25 minutes?
faq.answer: It is the conventional Pomodoro starting interval and gives the session a clear boundary. It is not a universal optimum. Adjust the block if your work or attention needs a different length.

faq.question: What should I do when I am interrupted?
faq.answer: Note the interruption briefly, handle it only if it cannot wait, and return to the intended outcome. Use repeated interruptions as a signal to change the environment or choose a more realistic focus window.

faq.question: Do I have to stop exactly when the timer ends?
faq.answer: No. The timer is a boundary for review, not a command to break useful flow. Reach a sensible stopping point, then decide deliberately whether to continue or take a break.

intro.html: A Pomodoro-style focus block is a simple way to put a boundary around one piece of work. Start with 25 minutes because it is an easy, familiar default, not because every task or person has the same ideal focus duration. The useful part is the loop: define an outcome, work with fewer competing inputs, stop to review, and adjust the next block.

sections.title: 1. Define one outcome
sections.html: Before starting the timer, write what should be different when the block ends. Prefer an observable outcome such as outline the first section, review these ten rows, or draft the reply over a vague label such as work on report.

sections.title: 2. Run one focus block
sections.html:
Set a 25-minute timer as the initial boundary. Keep only the material needed for the chosen outcome in front of you. If another task or idea appears, capture it in a short note instead of switching immediately.

If 25 minutes is clearly a poor fit for the work, use a different duration next time. The protocol is about deliberate focus blocks, not loyalty to a particular number.

sections.title: 3. Take a short break
sections.html: When you reach a stopping point, leave the task briefly. Stand up, get water, look away from the screen, or do another low-friction activity. The point is to create a real boundary before deciding what comes next.

sections.title: 4. Review before starting again
sections.html:
Use a short check-in:

  • Did I move the intended outcome forward?
  • What interrupted or slowed me?
  • Is another block on the same task useful?
  • Should the next block be shorter, the same, or longer?

Repeated friction is information. Change the task scope or environment rather than treating every imperfect block as a discipline failure.

sections.title: 5. Keep only the signal you need
sections.html: In Brali, put the intended outcome in a task or Focus session and use the check-in to record whether the block moved it forward and what interrupted you. You do not need a complicated productivity score. A few honest notes are enough to adjust the next block.

lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: In one conversation, wait until the other person finishes a thought, paraphrase the main point in your own words, invite correction, and ask one open question before offering advice or changing the topic.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Did I summarize before responding? Was my summary accepted or corrected, and what did the correction teach me?

faq.question: What if my summary is wrong?
faq.answer: That is useful feedback. Thank the person for correcting you, restate the point more accurately if needed, and continue from their correction rather than defending your first interpretation.

faq.question: Does active listening mean repeating the person's exact words?
faq.answer: No. Paraphrase the main point briefly in your own words. The goal is to test your understanding, not to imitate the speaker.

faq.question: Should I use a summary in every conversation?
faq.answer: No. Use it when understanding matters or you are unsure what the person means. If the situation requires immediate action or the person wants a direct answer, respond to that context instead of forcing a technique.

intro.html: Active listening can be practiced as a simple correction loop. Listen until the other person completes a thought, say back the main point in your own words, and give them room to confirm or correct you. The value is not in performing a perfect listening technique. It is in finding out whether your understanding matches what the other person meant.

sections.title: 1. Choose one conversation
sections.html: Pick a conversation where understanding matters: a work handoff, a disagreement, a planning discussion, or an ordinary conversation where you tend to jump to solutions. Your only practice goal is to test your understanding at least once when it feels useful.

sections.title: 2. Paraphrase the main point
sections.html:
After the person finishes a thought, summarize what you think the main point is in one short sentence. Use tentative language when you are unsure: If I understood you correctly… or So the main issue is…. Keep the summary shorter than the original explanation.

Avoid guessing motives or emotions as facts. If an interpretation matters, present it as a question that can be corrected.

sections.title: 3. Make correction easy
sections.html:
Pause after the summary and let the person respond. If they correct you, treat that as the success condition of the protocol: you discovered a mismatch before building the rest of the conversation on it.

You can use a short prompt such as Did I get that right? when confirmation is not obvious.

sections.title: 4. Ask one open question
sections.html: Once the main point is clear, ask one question that helps the person continue: What part matters most?, What happened next?, or What do you need from me here?. This prevents the listening exercise from turning into a sequence of summaries with no real conversation.

sections.title: 5. Review what you missed
sections.html:
After the conversation, record only the signal that helps the next attempt:

  • Did I summarize before jumping to advice?
  • Was my summary accepted or corrected?
  • If corrected, what assumption did I make too early?

In Brali, this can be one short check-in or journal note. You do not need to count eye-contact seconds, nods, or conversation scores.
